step1_summary: Chief complaint: Soreness, dryness, cracking, and occasional bleeding of the skin on fingers and palms, worsening over 3-4 months.

Symptoms: Dry, cracked, itchy skin on hands, mainly palms; symptoms started 3-4 months ago; itching intermittent; scratching sometimes causes bleeding; mild general skin dryness on legs but not severe; pain interfering with work; no systemic symptoms like fever, nausea, bowel or urinary problems.
Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; no known previous skin issues (eczema, dermatitis).
Medications/allergies: Metformin; no drug or other allergies.

Family/social history: Family history of diabetes; no known family skin disorders; non-smoker; minimal alcohol intake (a couple of pints a week); works as a hotel housekeeper; recently changed jobs 4 months ago; frequently uses cleaning products without consistent glove use.
Vital signs/exam findings: Not explicitly provided.

V: Peripheral vascular disease: Diabetes predisposes to microvascular complications that can impair skin integrity and healing, possibly contributing to dry, cracked skin.
I: Contact dermatitis (allergic or irritant): Exposure to cleaning chemicals without gloves can cause localized skin inflammation, dryness, itching, and cracking.
Fungal infection: Chronic moist/damaged skin may be secondarily infected, though no direct evidence in transcript.
N: Cutaneous lymphoma or neoplasm: Rare, but chronic skin changes could represent cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, though less likely without progressive severe symptoms.
D: Diabetic xerosis and neuropathy-related skin changes: Diabetes can cause dry skin due to autonomic dysfunction and neuropathy.
Nutritional deficiency (e.g., vitamin A, essential fatty acids): Could contribute to skin dryness but no dietary issues reported.
I2: Irritant reaction due to cleaning agents (chemical burns or dermatitis): Direct toxicity from cleaning products leading to irritant dermatitis.
C: Atopic dermatitis or inherited skin barrier disorders: Patient denies previous diagnosis; presentation at age 45 without prior history makes congenital causes less likely.
A: Autoimmune skin disease (e.g., psoriasis, lupus): Could cause chronic skin changes and cracking, but no reported systemic symptoms or typical rash distribution.
Allergic contact dermatitis: Immune-mediated reaction to chemicals at work, consistent with history.
T: Traumatic skin damage from frequent mechanical friction or washing related to housekeeping work: Could cause skin cracking and soreness.
E: Diabetes-related metabolic skin changes: Diabetes leads to dry skin and impaired wound healing.
Hypothyroidism: Can cause dry skin but no other hypothyroid symptoms reported.
